title: Supreme Court Orders DNA Tests, MEA Nodal Officer for Indians Killed in Russia-Ukraine War
excerpt: The court directed the government to help families identify mortal remains, file compensation claims and communicate in vernacular languages, as the Centre disclosed that 51 of 219 Indians who joined Russian forces are dead or missing.
body:
• India's Supreme Court has directed the MEA to appoint a nodal officer, arrange DNA profiling for families of Indians killed fighting in Russia's war on Ukraine, and assist with compensation claims.
  • Of 219 Indian nationals who joined Russian forces, 139 have been discharged and 51 are dead or missing; mortal remains of 29 have been returned so far.
  • Separately, four Indian seafarers were killed in a Russian missile strike on merchant vessel MV Golden Leo off Odesa in July, and 13 more remain stranded aboard MV AMIR1 at Chornomorsk port.
  • India has summoned both Russian and Ukrainian diplomats and condemned attacks on commercial shipping as 'deplorable.'

Court Issues Sweeping Directions

India's Supreme Court has issued a series of landmark directions aimed at protecting the families of Indian nationals caught up in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, ordering the Ministry of External Affairs to appoint a dedicated nodal officer and arrange DNA profiling to help identify the mortal remains of those killed while serving in Russian forces.

A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, alongside Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, was hearing a writ petition filed by family members of 26 Indian nationals who allege their relatives were lured to Russia with promises of well-paying jobs, only to have their passports confiscated and be forced into combat against Ukraine.

The government informed the court that of the 26 individuals named in the petition, 14 have died, 11 are missing in action, and one is incarcerated in a criminal case in Russia. Broadening the picture, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati disclosed that across all known cases, 219 Indian nationals joined Russian forces, of whom 139 have been discharged through diplomatic intervention, while 51 have died or remain unaccounted for. Mortal remains of 29 have been brought back to India.

Families Say Bodies Are Unidentifiable

The petitioners' counsel told the court that the bodies returned to families were often mutilated beyond recognition, and that the government had failed to collect DNA samples that would allow proper identification. The families alleged they had received no direct communication from the MEA despite repeated representations.

"We are stuck in Russia. We are fighting a war against Ukraine for a foreign state unwillingly."

— Petitioners' counsel, quoting stranded Indian nationals

The ASG countered that some families had refused to provide DNA samples and that repatriation of remains required a formal request from the families themselves. She also alleged that the petitioners' counsel had been posting videos on social media in connection with the case.

Cutting through the dispute, the bench issued four specific directions: the MEA must appoint a nodal officer whose contact details will be shared with all affected families; DNA tests of mortal remains must be conducted and matched with family members before bodies are handed over; the MEA must provide families with a complete procedure for filing compensation claims with Russian authorities; and the Legal Services Authority must provide free legal aid to affected families.

The court also directed the MEA to communicate with families in vernacular languages, recognising that many affected households would struggle with English-language official correspondence.

Seafarers Under Fire in the Black Sea

The Supreme Court case has unfolded against a backdrop of mounting danger to Indian civilians in and around the Ukraine conflict zone. On July 19, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged merchant vessel MV Golden Leo was struck by Russian cruise missiles while departing the port of Odesa, killing 10 people including four Indian seafarers. A fifth Indian crew member was hospitalised in critical condition.

It was the first confirmed instance of Indian seafarers being killed in the Russia-Ukraine war. India condemned the attack, with the MEA stating that targeting commercial shipping and endangering innocent civilian crew members is 'deplorable and should be avoided.'

Days later, the Forward Seamen's Union of India raised alarm over 13 Indian seafarers stranded aboard the cargo vessel MV AMIR1 at Ukraine's Chornomorsk port, where drone and missile attacks continued in the immediate vicinity. The Indian Embassy in Ukraine said it attached 'the highest priority' to the situation and was in constant touch with authorities.

Diplomatic Pushback on Both Sides

India's response has been notably even-handed. New Delhi summoned both Russian and Ukrainian diplomats to protest the repeated strikes affecting civilian merchant vessels and called for ensuring the safety of commercial shipping and civilian seafarers operating in international waters.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar separately communicated to Ukraine that attacks on Indian seafarers are 'unacceptable,' while the government has pressed Moscow on the plight of Indians recruited into Russian forces.

The case before the Supreme Court, DIVYA v. UNION OF INDIA (W.P.(C) No. 451/2026), has also raised allegations of human trafficking. The petitioners allege that recruitment agents operating in India channelled young men to Russia under false pretences, and that neither Indian nor Russian authorities have adequately investigated the trafficking networks involved.

What Comes Next

The court's directions place immediate obligations on the MEA to establish contact with affected families and begin DNA matching. Compensation claims, which Russia has indicated could include payments of approximately 1.5 crore rupees plus a monthly pension of 40,000 rupees per family, must now be facilitated through proper diplomatic channels. The matter remains before the court, with further hearings expected as the government files compliance reports.

For the Indian diaspora and maritime community, the escalating risks in the Black Sea remain a pressing concern. India has roughly 240,000 active seafarers — one of the largest contingents globally — and the safety of those operating near conflict zones has become a diplomatic priority that shows no sign of abating.
nri_angle: India has 240,000 active seafarers, many from diaspora-connected families; the Supreme Court case and Black Sea attacks directly affect NRI communities with relatives in maritime service.
